379.title: Gargi's second arrow
379.hook: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions
379.howItsDone: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka asked about the thread and the inner ruler, the one whose body the earth is. Your line was the inner ruler lives in every being.
screen: `THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Gargi stands up again. Two days ago she was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off, and she sat down. This time she speaks to the whole room first. Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya. As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.
screen: `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN.` → `A WARRIOR STRINGING HIS BOW.` → `TWO QUESTIONS, LIKE TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First arrow. What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows. Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow. And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers. That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. And yet at its command the sun and moon are held apart, earth and sky are held apart, and rivers run from the snowy mountains. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest. Brahman, the one reality, isn't one more thing in the world, not even the biggest thing. It's what everything is woven on, so the Upanishad describes it almost entirely by what it isn't. That's how many Hindus can bow to a murti of Krishna or Durga at home and still say God has no edges. As many teachers put it, the form is where you meet God, not a fence around God. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him. None of you will beat him. Then she falls silent, on her own terms. Tradition remembers her as a brahmavadini, a woman who spoke of Brahman, and she drew out the hardest answer of the day.

segments.voice: Sit, and let each thing you notice be named and set down: a sound, not that; a sensation in the knee, not that; a thought, not that. 380.title: How many gods? One
380.hook: the last challenger asks how many gods there are, and keeps asking until the number counts down to one
380.carry: truth is one; the wise call it many names
380.howItsDone: Hindu traditions hold many forms of the divine together with the conviction that the divine is one; ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti from the Rig Veda is often quoted for that idea, and the thirty-three gods are named in Vedic ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gargi's second arrow drew out the imperishable, brahman isn't one more thing. Your line was brahman isn't one more thing.

People sometimes say Hindus have three hundred thirty million gods. The Upanishad has its own count, and it's a countdown. The last challenger, Vidagdha Shakalya, asks Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, he answers. Yes, says Shakalya. But how many gods are there, really? Thirty-three. Yes, but how many really? Six. Really? Three. Really? Two. Really? One and a half. And how many gods are there, really? One.

Then Shakalya makes him explain each number. The three thousand and more, Yajnavalkya says, are only their powers. There are really thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, and Indra and Prajapati. The Vasus are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, sun, sky, moon and stars: everything dwells in them. The Rudras are the ten breaths in a person, and the self: when they leave the body, they make people weep. The Adityas are the twelve months, carrying everything along. Indra is the thunder; Prajapati is the sacrifice. The six are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, the sun and the sky. The three are the three worlds. The two are food and breath. The one and a half? The wind that blows, because everything grows in it. It's a pun in Sanskrit; it doesn't translate. And the one? Breath. It is Brahman. They call it That. Notice what didn't happen: the countdown never says the many gods were a mistake. They fold onto one, like a fan folding shut. A verse in the Rig Veda says it in a single line: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Hindus live this in different ways. Some worship one form of God as supreme, and see the others as that God's forms or helpers. Others honor many deities, each in its place. Advaita teachers hear in the count one reality appearing as many. This passage gives all of them room. So when a friend asks how many gods Hindus have, the honest answer is both: many forms, one truth.

381.title: Shakalya's last question
381.hook: the last challenger argues to win, the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him, and a riddle about a tree ends the debate
381.carry: the root of a person is knowing and joy
381.tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?
381.howItsDone: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses end the third book with a riddle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shakalya's countdown, from 3,306 gods all the way to one. Your line was truth is one; the wise call it many names.
screen: `TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one. Then, somewhere in the middle, he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?
screen: `HE DOESN'T SIT DOWN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?`

segments.voice: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them, to win. And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads. If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off. Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off: the text tells it in one plain sentence. Some readers take it literally, as the real stake of these Vedic debates; others hear an image: his whole argument came apart. Either way, set it beside Gargi. She got the same warning, stopped, and came back with better questions. Then Yajnavalkya asks the room one last riddle. A person is like a tree: hair for leaves, skin for bark, bones for the wood inside. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root. When death cuts a person down, from what root does he grow? Nobody in the room dares take him on. The chapter closes on its answer: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy. That's the teaching. Under everything you are, there's a root no argument and no death can cut, and it isn't dull or blank: it is awareness, and it is joy. Later Vedanta teachers gather this into a famous name for Brahman: sat-chit-ananda, being, awareness, joy. Shakalya staked his head on winning. The Upanishad says your root was never in the winning. Lose the argument, lose the job, lose someone you love: you've been cut down, not uprooted.
screen: `SENT IN TO WIN FOR THE OTHERS.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW, AND HIS HEAD FELL.` · `FROM WHAT ROOT DOES A PERSON GROW?` · `BRAHMAN: KNOWING, AND JOY.` · then, large: `THE ROOT OF A PERSON IS KNOWING AND JOY.`

382.title: The light of the self
382.hook: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
382.carry: the atman is a person's own light
382.tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world
382.howItsDone: Hindu homes and temples light lamps at dawn and dusk and at festivals, and teachers sometimes quote the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shakalya argued to win and lost his head, and the book ended with a tree. Your line was the root of a person is knowing and joy.
screen: `THE ROOT OF A PERSON IS KNOWING AND JOY.`

segments.voice: The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand. Then, from the next room, someone calls your name, and you get up and walk toward the voice. Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a talk between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows: King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T SEE YOUR HAND.` → `YOU WALK TOWARD THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have? The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True. But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire has gone out? Speech. That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya. And when the sun and the moon have set, the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati. The self is their light. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, the light within the heart. That's the teaching: the atman isn't something you see; it's the seeing, the light under all the others. You can watch Hindus live it. Many families light a diya, a small oil lamp, at the home shrine at dusk, and on Diwali they fill the house with them. Teachers often explain the outer flame as a reminder of this inner one. And a prayer many Hindus know by heart comes from this same Upanishad: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. Lead me from darkness to light.
screen: `THE SUN, THE MOON, THE FIRE.` · `SPEECH: WE WALK TOWARD A VOICE.` · `THE SELF IS THEIR LIGHT.` · `TAMASO MA JYOTIR GAMAYA.` · then, large: `THE ATMAN IS A PERSON'S OWN LIGHT.`

If you pray, say it once, softly: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. If not, just notice what's still lit.

383.title: The dreamer's own light
383.hook: there are no roads or chariots in a dream, and yet you ride one: who built it?
383.carry: the self lights even your dreams
383.tomorrow: deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved
383.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, laid out in this part of the Brihadaranyaka and in the Mandukya Upanishad, to point to the self that is present in all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: when the sun, moon, fire and speech are gone, the self is a person's light. Your line was the atman is a person's own light.
screen: `THE ATMAN IS A PERSON'S OWN LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Last night, maybe, you were at a train station you've never seen. Someone who died years ago was there, talking normally. The house you grew up in had an extra room. Nobody built that station, and there's no train in your bedroom. So where did it come from, and what was lighting it, with your eyes closed in a dark room? Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, turns to the place a sleeper goes at night.
screen: `A STATION YOU'VE NEVER SEEN.` → `NO TRAIN IN YOUR BEDROOM.` → `WHO BUILT IT?`

segments.voice: A person has two places, Yajnavalkya says: this world, and the other world. And there's a third, where the two meet: sleep, dreaming. Standing there, you can see both. When a person dreams, he takes the material of this whole world, tears it down himself, builds it up himself, and dreams by his own brightness, by his own light. There, the person is his own light. Then the famous passage. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses, roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights. But he makes joys, pleasures, delights. There are no ponds, no lakes, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lakes, rivers. For he is the maker. Notice two things. First, the building material is borrowed: the station is made out of stations you've seen, the face out of faces you know. Second, the light. The room is dark, the eyes are shut, and still everything is lit. People see his playground, the text says, but nobody sees him. Later Hindu schools argued over who really builds a dream, the dreamer or God. But this is the teaching they all keep: the atman is svayamjyoti, its own light. Awake, you borrow the sun's light; dreaming, nothing lights the scene but the self. Vedanta teachers walk through the three states, waking, dream and deep sleep, to make one point: the one who wakes, the one who dreams and the one who sleeps are the same self, there in all three. Your worst nightmare and your best day were lit by the same light.
screen: `THE THIRD PLACE: WHERE TWO WORLDS MEET.` · `NO CHARIOTS THERE; HE MAKES THEM.` · `BORROWED MATERIAL, HIS OWN LIGHT.` · `THE SAME SELF IN ALL THREE STATES.` · then, large: `THE SELF LIGHTS EVEN YOUR DREAMS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and build a place you love, slowly: a beach, a kitchen, a street, the color of the walls, the sound, the smell, all made of things you've seen. Dreaming. Where, Yajnavalkya says, the person is svayamjyoti, self-luminous, lit by its own light: no sun, no lamp, and still everything shows.

384.title: Deep sleep's embrace
384.hook: the best night's sleep you ever had, with nothing in it, and something that still woke up rested
384.carry: in deep sleep, the self is still there
384.tomorrow: death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade
384.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use deep sleep, described here and in the Mandukya Upanishad, as an everyday clue to the self: something rests, and on waking, one knows one slept well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dreaming. No chariots there, and the dreamer makes them, lit by the self. Your line was the self lights even your dreams.

Some nights you sleep so deeply there's nothing to report. No dream, no time passing, no you. Then the alarm, and you sit up and say, I slept like a stone. It's the best sleep there is, and nobody was there to enjoy it. Or was there? Who, exactly, slept well? Yajnavalkya takes King Janaka one floor below the dreams, to the place you go every night and never remember.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `I SLEPT LIKE A STONE.` → `WHO SLEPT WELL?`

segments.voice: As a falcon or an eagle, Yajnavalkya says, tired from circling all day in the sky, folds its wings and heads home to its nest, so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream. Then the image this day is named for. As a man held by the one he loves knows nothing outside and nothing inside, so a person held by the knowing self knows nothing outside and nothing inside. That is the form, the text says, where every desire is met, so there's no desire at all, and no sorrow. Then a startling list. There, a father is not a father, a mother not a mother. Gods are not gods. A thief is not a thief. Untouched by good, untouched by evil, he has crossed every sorrow of the heart. Nothing you are in daylight follows you in. And yet the text insists this isn't a blank. When he doesn't see there, he is still seeing, for the seer's seeing is never lost. There's just no second thing to see. Vedanta teachers draw a famous clue from this. You wake up and say, I slept well; I knew nothing. Who knew it was good? Someone was there: the self, resting with no roles at all. Not a daughter, not a student, not a worrier. That's the teaching: you are not your roles; the self is there even when every role is gone. In the Chandogya, Indra feared deep sleep was like being destroyed; here Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace. The Mandukya, which you met last year, names this state prajna, the third of the self's four quarters.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.` · `HELD, KNOWING NOTHING OUTSIDE OR IN.` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER.` · `I SLEPT WELL. WHO KNEW?` · then, large: `IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: Picture the falcon, tired, circling lower and lower, and with each out-breath fold something in: your plans for tonight, your name, your job, the role you play for other people. You're not trying to fall asleep, only letting the day's sky go, and resting in the nest with nothing outside to watch and nothing inside to fix.
Deep sleep. No dream, no desire, no sorrow: a person held by prajna, the knowing self, with nothing outside and nothing inside. In the Mandukya, the third state.
Your line: in deep sleep, the self is still there. The seer's seeing is never lost. Sleep well.

385.title: The caterpillar's crossing
385.hook: a small creature at the end of a blade of grass never lets go until it has hold of the next one
385.carry: death is a crossing, carrying what we did
385.tomorrow: "as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed"
385.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, are performed by the family with fire and mantras, and the days that follow include offerings for the departed; passages like this one and Bhagavad Gita 2.22 may be read or recalled at the time of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: deep sleep, the falcon folding its wings, held with no inside and no outside. Your line was in deep sleep, the self is still there.
screen: `IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: Crouch down in a garden and watch a caterpillar climb a blade of grass. At the tip, it doesn't fall off, and it doesn't jump. It stretches its front end out into the air, waving a little, until it touches the next blade. It grips. Only then does it let go of the old one and draw the rest of itself across. Yajnavalkya and King Janaka have walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Now the sage takes the last step, the one everyone takes, and he uses that caterpillar.
screen: `AT THE TIP OF A BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT REACHES, AND GRIPS.` → `ONLY THEN DOES IT LET GO.`

segments.voice: First he describes the dying, gently. The senses gather around the self, the way a king's officers gather when he's about to travel. Then the tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the self leaves, and the breath and the senses follow. And what goes with it? What it knew, and what it did, and what it had lived. Then the picture. As a caterpillar, coming to the end of a blade of grass, reaches out to another and draws itself across, so the self lays down this body, reaches out to another support and draws itself across. And one more: as a goldsmith hammers a piece of gold into a newer, more beautiful shape, so the self makes itself another form. This is the Hindu teaching of rebirth. Death isn't a fall into nothing. The self lets go of one body and crosses to the next, and what it carries is what it knew and what it did: its karma. You met Krishna's picture in the Gita last year, old clothes laid aside for new; it's the same teaching. It's why Hindu families gather for the last rites, antyeshti, with fire and prayers, and keep making offerings for the one who has gone: many understand it as helping someone across. This week: Gargi's arrows, one truth, the root, the self's light, dreams, deep sleep, and today, the crossing.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER; THE HEART LIGHTS UP.` · `THE CATERPILLAR REACHES THE NEXT BLADE.` · `REBIRTH, CARRYING KARMA.` · `ANTYESHTI: HELPING SOMEONE ACROSS.` · then, large: `DEATH IS A CROSSING, CARRYING WHAT WE DID.`

segments.voice: At the very end of each out-breath, notice the tiny reach toward the next breath; then let the old breath go, without hurrying it. If thoughts of death come, someone you've lost, or your own, let them be here too. If you pray, name the one you've lost and wish them a safe crossing; if not, just keep breathing, one blade to the next.
Death, as the Brihadaranyaka pictures it: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade of grass, reaching for the next before it lets go.
Your line: death is a crossing, carrying what we did. The gold is still the same gold. Day three hundred eighty-five, done.
